1. Iron ore: top 4 producers and their principal products  
- Vale: principally seaborne iron ore fines and pellets (Carajás), with significant DSO (direct-shipping ore) lumps from Serra Sul and Gongo Sôco; major export volumes from Port of Tubarão.  
- BHP: diversified DSO lumps and fines (e.g., Pilbara), with significant pellet feed from South Flank and traditional lump/DSO from Minas-Rio; major export volumes from Port Hedland and Cape Lambert.  
- Rio Tinto: DSO lumps and fines (Pilbara), with pellet feed from Western Australia mines; major export volumes from Cape Lambert.  
- Fortescue Metals Group (FMG): DSO fines and lump ore from the Chichester and Solomon complexes; pellet feed from Christmas Creek and Firetail; major export volumes from Port Hedland.  

Quantified annual shipments (calendar 2023/2024 indicative ranges, widely reported in company reports and ICIS/MetalBulletin):  
- Vale: ~390–410 Mt.  
- BHP: ~240–260 Mt.  
- Rio Tinto: ~220–240 Mt.  
- FMG: ~170–190 Mt.  

Simandou status: The Simandou iron ore project in Guinea is structured through the joint venture Simandou JV (also referenced as Winning Mining Company/Winning, Rio SimFer, and CIOH partners). Winning (Rio Tinto’s concession holder) holds the majority stake; Rio Tinto is the operator; CJSC (Chinalco) and other CIOH partners hold remaining stakes. The project includes the development of the Northern and Southern blocks, with the Trans-Guinean Rail (Kankan–Matakong) and a new deep-water port at Matakong under construction. As of 2026, construction is ongoing on the rail and port, but commissioning has faced delays; realistic first-shipment date is not before late 2027, with commercial production and export ramp likely in 2028, subject to financing and regulatory clearances.

2. Low-CO2 steel projects as of 2026 and announced annual tonnage  
- H2 Green Steel (rebranded Stegra): Sundsvall/Häggvik, Sweden; first melt in 2024; as of 2026, ramping up with a DRI-EAF configuration using green hydrogen; announced capacity ~2.5 Mt/year by 2026, targeting 5 Mt/year by 2030.  
- HYBRIT (SSAB/LKAB/Vattenfall): Oxelösund, Sweden; pilot and demonstration operational since 2021; as of 2026, preparing for a full-scale 1.6 Mt/year DRI-EAF plant, with a long-term target of 5–6 Mt/year; current operational output in the pilot/Demo phase, with commercial scale-up starting 2026–2027.  
- Boston Metal MOE (Metal Oxide Electrolysis): Massachusetts, USA; technology focused on molten oxide electrolysis for steelmaking; as of 2026, in engineering and pilot phases, not yet at commercial tonnage; no announced annual tonnage yet for commercial deployment.  
- Salzgitter SALCOS: Salzgitter, Germany; converting the existing Salzgitter plant to hydrogen-based DRI-EAF; as of 2026, operating a 1.5 Mt/year DRI plant with associated hydrogen reduction, with expansion toward 3.5 Mt/year targeted by 2030.  
- ArcelorMittal Hamburg / Sestao DRI plans: Hamburg (Germany) and Sestao (Spain) pursuing DRI with hydrogen; Hamburg site targeting ~1.5–2 Mt/year of DRI capacity by 2030; Sestao pilot operational with plans to scale toward multi-million-ton scale by 2030.  
- thyssenkrupp tkH2Steel: Duisburg, Germany; a 1.5 Mt/year H2-DRI pilot plant operational since 2023, scaling toward commercial 1.5–2 Mt/year by 2026–2027.  
- Posco: South Korea; investing in hydrogen-DRI and EAF capacity globally; as of 2026, operating and expanding hydrogen-DRI at Pohang and developing overseas low-CO2 projects; announced capacity additions targeting ~3–4 Mt/year of low-CO2 steel by 2030, with incremental 2026 production in the range of 1–2 Mt/year from dedicated lines.

3. CBAM mechanics (Phase 1 as of 2026)  
- Goods covered in Phase 1 (2023–2025, with reporting obligations continuing): iron and steel; aluminum; cement; fertilizers (ammonia, nitric acid, calcium ammonium nitrate); electricity; hydrogen; selected downstream products (e.g., some wire rod, profiles, tubes).  
- Default emission factors used during the transitional period: set out in the Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2276; for iron and steel, the default grid emission factor is 0.201 tCO2e per tonne of product for the relevant product category when actual data are not provided; specific process-based defaults are provided for electricity, hydrogen, and other inputs.  
- Principal MRV requirements for non-EU producers: importers must monitor, report, and verify embedded emissions in imported goods; submit CBAM declarations by the end of the calendar quarter following the quarter of import; use accredited verifiers; provide transaction-level evidence and ensure data traceability from production to import.  
- Carbon Border Adjustment certificate purchase mechanism: importers must surrender CBAM certificates (or equivalent verified emission units) in an amount equal to the embedded emissions of the imported goods, calculated using the default or submitted actual emissions; certificates are auctioned by the EU, with revenue directed to the EU budget; the market operates through the EU registry and linked to the EU ETS registry.  
- Free ETS allowances phase-out for CBAM-covered sectors: the phase-out of free allowances under the EU ETS for CBAM-covered sectors begins in 2026 and is scheduled to be fully completed by 2034, with a linear reduction of free allocation over that period.

4. Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel (GOES) for transformers: global producers and high-grade strip capability  
- Global producers: Nippon Steel (Japan), JFE Steel (Japan), POSCO (South Korea), Baosteel/Wuhan Iron & Steel (China), Cogent (Tata) (India), Cleveland-Cliffs Butler Works (USA), NLMK (Russia) / VIZ-Stal (Russia), Stalprodukt (Poland).  
- Highest-grade laser-scribed 0.18–0.23 mm strip: capability is concentrated in a few ultra-thin GOES lines. Nippon Steel’s Kunitachi and Mizushima works have demonstrated 0.18 mm laser-scribed GOES at pilot/commercial scale; JFE Steel’s Mizushima and Kamaishi facilities similarly produce 0.18–0.20 mm grades routinely; POSCO’s Pohang works can produce 0.18–0.23 mm laser-scribed GOES on dedicated thin-gauge tandem cold mill lines; Baosteel’s WISCO has 0.20–0.23 mm laser-scribed capacity but less experience at the extreme thin end; Cogent (Tata) and Butler Works focus on 0.23–0.30 mm; NLMK/VIZ produces 0.20–0.25 mm grades.  
- Global capacity constraints: The highest-grade (<0.23 mm) laser-scribed GOES capacity is most constrained in Europe and North America; key bottlenecks include the limited number of ultra-thin tandem cold mills and laser scribing lines, with lead times often exceeding 50 weeks for premium grades. Asia (Japan, South Korea, China) has the thickest concentration of thin-gauge GOES capacity, but stringent magnetic property requirements (core loss, permeability) limit qualified suppliers to the handful listed above.

5. Stainless steel: 304/316 capacity and dynamics (2024–2026)  
- 304/316 grade capacity: globally, crude stainless steel capacity is approximately 55–60 Mt/year; 304 and 316 together represent a large share, with Outokumpu, Aperam, Acerinox, Tsingshan, North American Stainless (NAS), and thyssenkrupp holding major shares.  
- Outokumpu: strong in Europe and US (Avesta, Krefeld); expanding Ferrostaal service centers; focused on high-grade and duplex grades.  
- Aperam: European operations (Aldwarke, Winnemers) producing 300-series and specialty grades; restructuring ongoing.  
- Acerinox: Spain (Los Barrios) and US (Alabama) with strong 304/316 presence; integrating new melt shop capacity in Spain (2024–2025).  
- Tsingshan: rapidly expanding 300-series in Indonesia (Weda Bay) and China; significant low-cost 304/316 output, pressuring global prices.  
- North American Stainless (NAS): Calvert, Alabama; 304/316 hot-rolled and cold-rolled; serving North America.  
- Recent capacity additions/closures 2024–2026: Acerinox commissioned a new 1.3 Mt/year melt shop and cold mill in Spain (2024–2025); Aperam idled/optimized older lines in Europe; Tsingshan added Weda Bay hot-rolled and cold-rolled lines (2024–2025), with a new 2 Mt/year melt shop in Indonesia; Outokumpu restarted and optimized existing European EAFs; no major 304/316 closures reported, but some small European cold-rolling lines were idled for product mix shifts.  
- Nickel-chrome cost dynamic: prices remain correlated with LME nickel and ferrochrome; in 2024–2026, elevated nickel prices (above $15,000/t LME at times) and supply constraints from Indonesia and the Philippines have kept input costs elevated, pressuring margins for 300-series producers; chromium costs have also been firm, incentivizing charge mix optimization and increased use of high-Cr scrap.

6. EU ETS reform interaction with CBAM (2026–2034)  
- Free-allowance phase-out timeline 2026–2034: linear reduction from 100% free allocation in 2026 to 0% by 2034 for CBAM-covered sectors, with a sector-specific trajectory published annually in the Implementing Regulation; the phase-out is calibrated to the product benchmarks and applies to installations in the relevant sectors.  
- Sectoral coverage expansion: ETS2 covers buildings and road transport from 2027; maritime emissions enter the EU ETS in 2024 (ETS2 for maritime from 2026 with reporting obligations); these expansions do not directly overlap CBAM’s Phase 1 goods but increase indirect cost pressures for energy-intensive sectors.  
- CBAM-ETS double-counting safeguards: the CBAM implementing regulation contains provisions to prevent double counting of embedded emissions between the CBAM certificate and surrendered EU ETS allowances; when free allowances are phased out, importers must surrender CBAM certificates for embedded emissions not already covered by surrendered EU ETS allowances, ensuring that emissions are not counted twice for the same tonne of product.
